k-1.x_notes: Strengths: clean and format-compliant (consistent header/footer, plain 'Problem N:' text, no Name field, no talk boxes or cheerleading). All shapes are actual size and correct: the sailboat (11 triangles), cat (7), hexagon and side-2 diamond, the chevron arrow (2 chevrons) and hexagram star (3 chevrons, which works by pairing adjacent point-rhombi), the 2-1-1 long hexagon in blues (3 tilings), and the side-3 mountain. The chevron-only star is a real little puzzle. Weaknesses: every task is 'fill it' with no counting, comparing, recording or optimizing. 'Then fill it again with any small pieces you like' is filler, and 'mountain with only greens' is trivial. Nothing connects to the session's kernel (for example, blues on a triangle and the leftover gaps), and the upscale blocks go unused. The shapes are small, so the band is at real risk of the 'too dumbed down, ends too early' failure the organizer complains about.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: real mathematics at a K-1 entry point, with a clear development. Children count greens on block outlines, fill a hexagon many ways (six recording boards, chevron+blue also works), and fill a hexagram any way and then blues only (6 blues, forced and unique). Big triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 take 4, 9 and 16 greens and use the 2x and 3x upscale greens. Covering those triangles with blues and the fewest greens gives 2, 3, 4, a genuine kernel-1 pattern. Boards are actual size, with dotted guide grids and number boxes that suit pre-readers, and the block icons help non-readers. It should fill 40 minutes. Weaknesses: Name field, a title above every problem, a 'Talk about it' box on every page (adult prompts on the student page), a 'Your turn!' box, exclamation-mark cheerleading ('Cover it all up!'), a non-standard footer, and a 'One way: 2 reds' example. Problem 1 (single-block outlines) is very easy.
k-1.reason: Y gives kindergartners and first graders counting, comparing and a real fewest-gaps pattern for the full working time. X is tidy but is only a run of fill-the-shape tasks with no kernel connection, which is exactly the thin K-1 page the organizer has complained about. Y's clutter (Name, titles, talk boxes) can be deleted in the editing window. X's missing content cannot be added in that time.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: clean, compliant and discovery-oriented. Three substantial problems with plenty of hands-on work: possible/impossible boards; best blue packings of triangles of side 2 to 5 (1/2, 3/3, 6/4, 10/5 empty), ending with 'explain why you cannot leave fewer'; and six boards tried first with blues and then with chevrons. On those boards A and C give 0/0, B gives 0 vs 4, D gives 0 vs 2, E gives 1/1, and F (even area, 5 up and 3 down) gives 2 vs 4. That covers the chevron part of the kernel well. All boards are actual size and every answer checks. The method stays open; nothing hands over the up/down idea. Weaknesses: in Problem 1 both impossible boards (A, 9 triangles; C, 11) have odd area, so the warm-up's 'what is stopping you' answer is just parity and misses the even-area obstruction at the start. The up/down argument must come from the adult at the 'explain why' prompts. There is some repeated wording (rules restated in each problem, and 'Problem 2' relabelled on the continuation page).
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: a very well-developed kernel-1 sequence with contrasting examples. Children dot the up-triangles and tabulate up/down coverage by each block, then decide possible/impossible on even-area boards (side-2 triangle 3/1, inverted trapezoid 3/5, hexagram 6/6, long hexagon 5/5). The broken hexagons (22 white each; X removes two ups and is impossible, Y removes an up and a down and is tileable, checked) are a true mutilated-checkerboard analogue. Fewest gaps for sides 2 to 5 lead to a prediction table for 6 and 10. All mathematics checks and the boards are actual size. Weaknesses: it gives the thinking away. The up/down invariant is front-loaded as a directed step, 'leaves only as many gaps as the side length' states the discovery, and '(Hint: each blue covers one up and one down)' prints the proof. It also has a Name field, titles, a 'Talk about it' box on every page, and 'Make your own' and 'Purple puzzle' labels. Chevrons are reduced to a sidebar.
grades-2-3.reason: Y's arc is mathematically richer, but its pages walk third graders straight to the coloring argument and are full of the boxes and hints the organizer rejects. X keeps the discovery open, is clean, and gives the chevron comparison real hands-on weight. Its main flaw is the odd-area warm-up boards.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: clean, compliant and mathematically correct throughout. The 1-2-2 tall hexagon is at actual size, with eight small recording boards and an efficient record-by-joining-centers method. The six printed cards are exactly the six tilings (codes RRLL, RLRL, LRRL, RLLR, LRLR, LLRR, checked), and the A-to-B flip demo matches them. Questions cover connectivity, the shortest route A to F (4 flips), odd round trips, ribbon uniqueness, matching the C(4,2) words to cards, rebuilding a tiling from its ribbon (both drawn ribbons valid), and 'a flip swaps an adjacent LR pair'. Weaknesses: page 2 prints all six tilings right after Problem 1 asks children to find them, which undercuts the central search, and nothing asks how they know they have them all. The work is fragmented into ten mostly small, directed problems (circle every RL, write three examples). It stays on one 6-tiling hexagon with no 3D/cube view and no larger case to extend strong students.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: a fuller and deeper arc. A warm-up on the unit hexagon (exactly two tilings, correct) introduces the flip and the 3D view, with consistent shading. Children find all tilings of the tall hexagon themselves and are asked 'are you sure there are no more? why?'. They build a flip map from their own tilings. The fewest flips from X (LLRR) to Y (RRLL) is 4, with 'how do you know' (checked). Round trips lead to ribbon words that settle the count at 6, and the L-score gives a parity proof that no round trip is odd (the example LRRL scores 5). The 2-2-2 big hexagon (actual size) uses two non-crossing ribbons. The example tiling with left LRLR and right RLRL is valid and the 3D example has a consistent 4/4/4 shading. Counting its 20 tilings gives the 5th grader an extension. Weaknesses: Name field, titles, a 'Coming up ... secret code' teaser, a 'Tips' box with group roles and a 'flip them!' hint, 'Challenge.' labels, and sub-numbered steps inside problems. The L-score is supplied rather than discovered.
grades-4-5.reason: Y lets children find and then prove the full set of tall-hexagon tilings, gives a proof of flip parity, and extends to the 20-tiling big hexagon and the cube picture. X gives away its own central search on page 2 and splinters the rest into small steps. Y's decorative boxes and teaser can be cut in a few minutes.

overall.reason: Y's mathematical content is clearly stronger for K-1 (a real fewest-gaps idea and a full hour of work) and for grades 4-5 (a self-found tiling count, a parity proof and the big-hexagon extension), and all of it checks. Its faults are mostly removable clutter: Name fields, titles, talk boxes, teasers and hints. X is the cleaner, more compliant packet and slightly better for grades 2-3, but its K-1 is thin and its 4-5 prints the answer to its own central search, and those gaps cannot be fixed in fifteen minutes.
